text: Time to put exact numbers side by side. This lab walks through classical and quantum information using the same small system size, n equals 3, so you can see precisely where they match, where they diverge, and why that divergence is the idea the rest of this course keeps coming back to.

Three classical bits have 2 cubed, or 8, possible configurations, but the system is only ever in exactly one of those 8 at a time, so 3 bits of memory fully describes it. Three qubits are different: their state vector lives in an 8-dimensional complex space, written as c-zero times ket 000 plus c-one times ket 001, all the way through c-seven times ket 111 — 8 complex amplitudes, one for every 3-bit string, constrained so the sum of their squared magnitudes equals 1.

Take the uniform superposition, where every one of those 8 amplitudes is equal to 1 over root 8, about 0.35355. Squaring that gives a probability of 0.125, or one-eighth, for each of the 8 outcomes, and summing all 8 of those gives exactly 1, confirming the state is valid. Measuring this system gives one of the 8 three-bit strings, each equally likely — statistically identical to flipping 3 fair coins.

Here's the tension, stated precisely. Representing n qubits in full generality takes 2 to the n amplitudes — 10 qubits need 1,024, 50 qubits need over a quadrillion, far beyond anything classical storage can hold directly. But reading out that system gives you exactly n classical bits per measurement, no matter how large n gets. That gap is exactly why quantum computers can be powerful, since algorithms exploit that exponential structure through interference, and exactly why they're hard to simulate classically, since tracking all those amplitudes exactly hits that same exponential wall.
That closes out classical versus quantum information. Chapter 2 starts applying real operations to a qubit's state vector, beginning with the Pauli gates, X, Y, and Z.
